paragraphs.heading: What organic reactions are
paragraphs.text: Organic reactions are chemical reactions that involve organic compounds. Chemists use them to build new organic molecules, and the making of drugs, plastics, food additives and fabrics relies on them. Some are very old, such as burning organic fuels and turning fats into soap, which is called saponification. Modern organic chemistry begins with the Wöhler synthesis of 1828.

paragraphs.heading: Sorting by what happens
paragraphs.text: The basic types are addition, elimination, substitution, pericyclic, rearrangement, photochemical and redox reactions. Some reactions fit more than one type; certain substitutions, for example, go by way of an addition followed by an elimination. Another way to sort them is by the reagent a change needs. The main kinds are oxidizing agents like osmium tetroxide, reducing agents like lithium aluminium hydride, bases like lithium diisopropylamide and acids like sulfuric acid.

paragraphs.heading: Reactions with names
paragraphs.text: Organic chemists like to name a reaction after the person or people who invented it, and a cautious count of these named reactions comes to 1000. The Claisen rearrangement of 1912 is an old one, and the Bingel reaction of 1993 a recent one. Several have earned the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, among them the Grignard reaction (1912), the Diels–Alder reaction (1950), the Wittig reaction (1979) and olefin metathesis (2005).

paragraphs.heading: Three classes of mechanism
paragraphs.text: Each reaction has a mechanism, the series of steps that explains how it happens, and reactions are also grouped by it into three common classes. In polar reactions, which are the vast majority, a pair of electrons moves from a clear source, such as a lone pair, to a clear sink, an electrophilic center. In radical reactions, species with unpaired electrons, called radicals, move single electrons, in chain or nonchain processes. Pericyclic reactions shuffle bonds around a cyclic transition state, with electron pairs moving in a loop that has no true source or sink. Some processes mix steps from two or even all three classes.

paragraphs.heading: What steers a reaction
paragraphs.text: Organic reactions are governed by much the same factors as any chemical reaction. Particular to them are things that set how stable reactants and products are, such as conjugation and aromaticity, and reactive intermediates such as free radicals, carbocations and carbanions. Because one organic compound can come as many isomers, selectivity matters a great deal: regioselectivity, diastereoselectivity and enantioselectivity. The Woodward–Hoffmann rules govern the stereochemistry of pericyclic reactions, and Zaitsev's rule that of many eliminations.

paragraphs.heading: Making medicines
paragraphs.text: Organic reactions are important in making pharmaceuticals. A 2006 review estimated that 20% of the chemical conversions were alkylations on nitrogen and oxygen atoms. Another 20% put on or took off protective groups, 11% made new carbon–carbon bonds, and 10% turned one functional group into another.

paragraphs.heading: Water, chains and arrows
paragraphs.text: In a condensation reaction two reactants combine and give off a small molecule, usually water. The opposite, where a reaction uses up water, is hydrolysis. Many polymerizations come from organic reactions, and they split into addition polymerizations and step-growth polymerizations. To show a mechanism step by step, chemists use arrow pushing: curved arrows that track how electrons move as starting materials turn into intermediates and products.
